pamphlet_excerpts: Tool Storage Safety: Place garden rakes and hoes with tines pointed downward into soil.
Hydration Maintenance: Drink eight ounces of cool potable water every thirty minutes outdoors.
Tetanus Protection Protocol: Clean puncture wounds immediately with soap and water before seeking medical care.
Personal Protective Equipment: Wear heavy leather gloves and broad brimmed hats under direct sun.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Protective Gear Selection: Put on sturdy work boots, leather gloves, and UV protective safety glasses.
Step 2 - Tool Cutting Inspection: Sharpen dull hand pruners and tighten loose pivot nuts before working.
Step 3 - Plot Debris Clearing: Remove broken glass, hidden scrap metal, and thorned branches from paths.
Step 4 - Sanitizing Puncture Wounds: Flush abrasions with clean tap water and dress them with sterile gauze.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Floral Anatomy Examination: Identify stamens, anthers, pistils, and nectar glands on open crop blooms.

comparison_data.right_header: Wild Pollinators Like Bats and Birds
left_points: Ancient Human Bee Partnership: You may have never thought much about honey bees, but there has been a strong relationship between bees and humans for thousands of years (p. 59).
Pollinator Importance for Food: Without these winged creatures, many of our food sources would be in great peril (p. 59).
Crop and Feed Pollination: We rely on honeybees not only for the sweet honey they make, but more importantly for their ability to pollinate many of the crops and livestock feed (p. 59).
right_points: Step 1 - Recognize Crop Pollination Value: We rely on honeybees not only for the sweet honey they make, but more importantly for their ability to pollinate many of the crops and livestock feed (p. 59).

Step 2 - Observe Flower Pollen Transfer: Some plants can produce seeds only if pollen is exchanged between flowers on the same plant, or from flowers of different plants from the same variety (p. 59).
Step 3 - Identify Diverse Native Pollinators: Birds, bats, bumblebees, butterflies, and many other creatures help transfer pollen as they flit from flower to flower or feed on the nectar (p. 59).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following and record weekly observations. Discuss the results of your project with your counselor. (a) Build a compost bin and maintain it for 90 days. (b) Build a vermicompost bin (worm compost bin) and maintain it for 90 days. (c) Build a hydroponic garden containing three vegetables or herbs, or three ornamental plants. Maintain this garden through harvest or flowering, or for 90 days. (d) Build one water garden, either in a container (at least 12 by 6 inches and 6 inches deep), or in the ground as a small, decorative pond no larger than 6 by 3 feet and 24 inches deep. Maintain the water garden for 90 days. (e) Prepare a honey super for use on a hive or colony. Remove a filled honey super from the hive or colony and prepare the honey for sale. (f) Grow a garden of your own using soil from seed or plantings to harvest or for 90 days, whichever is earlier. This can be an outdoor garden or indoors using appropriate containers, and should include at least three types of plants approved by your counselor.

Step 4 - Weekly Observation Tracking: Record structural changes, biological activity, and chemical conditions across ninety days.

left_points: (8a) Aerobic Compost Bin Construction: Aerobic composting combines carbon rich brown materials with nitrogen rich green materials. Regular turning injects atmospheric oxygen to feed heat producing thermophilic decomposers.

(8b) Vermicomposting Bin System Care: Vermiculture uses specialized Eisenia fetida worms to process kitchen vegetable scraps into castings. Managing bedding moisture and neutral pH prevents anaerobic odors in the bin.

(8c) Hydroponic Garden System Maintenance: Hydroponic farming suspends plant roots in oxygenated nutrient solution without traditional soil media. Managing water temperature, dissolved salts, and light cycles ensures vigorous vegetable production.
right_points: (8d) Aquatic Water Garden Design: Water gardens balance aquatic plants, surface shading, and biological filtration in a shallow reservoir. Establishing biological equilibrium prevents stagnant conditions while creating microhabitats for beneficial wildlife.

(8e) Honey Super Hive Management: Beekeepers add honey supers above queen excluders to harvest surplus nectar converted to honey. Extracting, filtering, and bottling honey requires sanitary handling and moisture testing under eighteen percent.

(8f) Ninety Day Garden Production: Cultivating a dedicated plot or container garden demonstrates season long crop management skills. Regular watering, staking, mulching, and weeding sustain plant vitality through the harvest period.

pamphlet_excerpts: Lineage Science: Genealogy systematically traces bloodlines and legal relationships across multiple successive historical eras.
Pedigree Documentation: Ancestor charts record direct biological antecedents while descendant charts track succeeding generational offspring.
Vital Registration: Family group sheets capture vital statistics for parents and children within households.
Standard Nomenclature: Standardized genealogical terminology prevents confusion between direct forebears and collateral family lines.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Define Terms: Write precise operational definitions for genealogy, ancestor, and descendant in your field notebook.
Step 2 - Structure Pedigree: Sketch a basic ancestral pedigree chart tracing biological lineage back through great-grandparents.
Step 3 - Draft Household: Enter complete vital statistics for a single nuclear family onto group sheets.
Step 4 - Review Formats: Compare linear pedigree charts against multi-generational family group sheets with your counselor.

options: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
B. A primary source is any story repeated at a family reunion fifty years later, whereas a secondary source is a courthouse marriage license signed by the officiating judge.
C. A primary source refers only to relatives on your father's side, whereas a secondary source refers to relatives on your mother's side.
D. Secondary sources are always 100 percent error-free and never need to be verified against vital records or federal census schedules.

pamphlet_excerpts: Chronological Sequencing: Structured timelines reveal geographic migrations and historical context across an individual human life.
Primary Source Creation: Consistent personal journaling preserves contemporary firsthand eyewitness testimony for future historical researchers.
Contextual Synthesis: Correlating family events with local historical crises illuminates ancestral decisions and community relocations.

Step 4 - Maintain Journal: Log weekly personal reflections, community events, and family observations over six consecutive weeks.

Evidentiary Evaluation: Primary information recorded near the event time carries higher reliability than delayed recollections.
Jurisdictional Targeting: Civil birth certificates reside with county registrars while historic land patents occupy state archives.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Repositories: Locate three physical archives and three digital record databases applicable to your family.

Step 4 - Map Records: List standard municipal, religious, and federal repositories for birth, marriage, and death records.

Repository Access: Public archives maintain probate records, tax rolls, and land deeds within reading rooms.
Professional Expertise: Certified genealogists offer specialized linguistic, paleographic, and jurisdictional search services for complex lineage problems.
Query Protocol: Formal research inquiries should specify exact names, geographic localities, and narrow historical timeframes.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select Entity: Choose one genealogical society, certified professional, or historical repository relevant to family origins.
Step 2 - Formulate Inquiry: Prepare specific questions about their holdings, access policies, search fees, and research services.
Step 3 - Transmit Query: Contact the selected institution or specialist via telephone, email, or formal postal letter.
Step 4 - Document Response: Record the organization's service offerings, archival holdings, and research guidance in your notebook.

pamphlet_excerpts: Exponential Growth: Every generation doubles ancestral lines, requiring two parents and four biological grandparents on charts.
Standard Dates: Record dates using day, three-letter month abbreviation, and four-digit year format consistently.
Standard Places: List geographic locations in ascending hierarchical order from town, to county, state, country.
Maiden Names: Always record females using their maiden surnames rather than their married legal surnames.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Position Self: Enter your complete legal name, birth date, and birthplace on line one.
Step 2 - Record Parents: Add father's details on upper line two and mother's details on lower line.
Step 3 - Add Grandparents: Enter verified vital details for paternal and maternal grandparents on lines four through seven.
Step 4 - Verify Completeness: Check every chart entry for standard date formatting, maiden names, and complete localities.

Step 3 - Rule Out False Matches: In fact, it is possible that none of the matches you get will be your ancestor (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Household Completeness: Family group sheets capture all children, including those who died during infancy or childhood.
Chronological Sibling Sequence: List children in strict birth order regardless of gender to maintain accurate generational chronology.
Marriage Documentation: Document exact marriage dates, officiants, witnesses, and civil jurisdictions for the parental couple.
Dual Record Linking: Linking generational family group records creates continuous documentation across successive family households.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Draft Personal Household: List your parents as the couple and yourself with your siblings as children.
Step 2 - Record Parental Household: Create a second sheet showing a parent and their siblings as the children.
Step 3 - Enter Vital Dates: Fill in birth, marriage, and death dates with exact locations for every person.
Step 4 - Cross-Reference Records: Link the child on the older sheet to the parent on the newer sheet.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
options: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
B. A primary source is any story repeated at a family reunion fifty years later, whereas a secondary source is a courthouse marriage license signed by the officiating judge.
C. A primary source refers only to relatives on your father's side, whereas a secondary source refers to relatives on your mother's side.
D. Secondary sources are always 100 percent error-free and never need to be verified against vital records or federal census schedules.

A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Genealogists distinguish original, contemporaneous primary records (vital certificates, wills, census returns) from derivative or secondary compilations, cross-checking facts to build an accurate pedigree and family group record.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why does the Genealogy merit badge pamphlet recommend starting your family history research with your own life story?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why does the Genealogy merit badge pamphlet recommend starting your family history research with your own life story?
options: A. Your own history is the easiest place to start and builds habits for recording facts and stories
B. Public archives require a personal biography before granting access to census rolls
C. Genealogy software programs lock out ancestor entries until a six-week diary is uploaded
D. Personal timelines automatically verify the birth certificates of your great-grandparents
choices: A. Your own history is the easiest place to start and builds habits for recording facts and stories
B. Public archives require a personal biography before granting access to census rolls
C. Genealogy software programs lock out ancestor entries until a six-week diary is uploaded
D. Personal timelines automatically verify the birth certificates of your great-grandparents
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Your own history is the easiest place to start and builds habits for recording facts and stories
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Starting with your own history is the easiest entry point into genealogy and lets you practice organizing timelines, biographies, and journals using events you already know firsthand (p. 11).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When interviewing relatives about family history, which type of information is most likely to be remembered accurately compared to specific dates and places?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When interviewing relatives about family history, which type of information is most likely to be remembered accurately compared to specific dates and places?
options: A. Exact street addresses from childhood homes
B. Precise years of marriage and naturalization
C. Family relationships, such as who was a grandparent's sibling
D. Original spellings of towns in foreign countries
choices: A. Exact street addresses from childhood homes
B. Precise years of marriage and naturalization
C. Family relationships, such as who was a grandparent's sibling
D. Original spellings of towns in foreign countries
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Family relationships, such as who was a grandparent's sibling
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): In oral interviews, family relationships (such as knowing that great-uncle Ralph was Grandpa Erickson's brother) are usually reliable, whereas exact names, places, and dates are more often misremembered (p. 17).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In the United States today, which level of government is primarily responsible for creating and issuing official birth, marriage, and death vital records?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In the United States today, which level of government is primarily responsible for creating and issuing official birth, marriage, and death vital records?
options: A. The federal National Archives
B. Each individual state government
C. The U.S. Census Bureau
D. International lineage societies
choices: A. The federal National Archives
B. Each individual state government
C. The U.S. Census Bureau
D. International lineage societies
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Each individual state government
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In the United States, each state creates and maintains the basic vital records for births, marriages, and deaths occurring within its borders (p. 20).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the main purpose of an ancestral family organization built around an early founding couple?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the main purpose of an ancestral family organization built around an early founding couple?
options: A. Issuing legal birth and marriage certificates on behalf of state governments
B. Charging mandatory membership fees to anyone born with that surname
C. Replacing federal census records with private family guesswork
D. Researching the ancestry and descendants of that couple and sharing the verified information
choices: A. Issuing legal birth and marriage certificates on behalf of state governments
B. Charging mandatory membership fees to anyone born with that surname
C. Replacing federal census records with private family guesswork
D. Researching the ancestry and descendants of that couple and sharing the verified information
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Researching the ancestry and descendants of that couple and sharing the verified information
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Ancestral family organizations bring together descendants of a specific couple to conduct quality research into the couple's ancestry and descendants and share those records (p. 19).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How can you narrow an online genealogy search when typing an ancestor's name returns thousands of results?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How can you narrow an online genealogy search when typing an ancestor's name returns thousands of results?
options: A. Remove the surname and search only by the ancestor's first name
B. Accept the first result listed at the top of the search engine page
C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
D. Search only for living relatives instead of historical records
choices: A. Remove the surname and search only by the ancestor's first name
B. Accept the first result listed at the top of the search engine page
C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
D. Search only for living relatives instead of historical records
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Adding specific keywords like the place or year an ancestor died narrows thousands of broad hits down to records that are much more likely to match the right person (p. 16).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: On the second family group record form required in Requirement 7, who is listed in the children's section?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: On the second family group record form required in Requirement 7, who is listed in the children's section?
options: A. Yourself and your first cousins
B. Your parent or guardian along with his or her brothers and sisters
C. All four of your grandparents from both sides of the family
D. Your great-grandparents and their neighbors
choices: A. Yourself and your first cousins
B. Your parent or guardian along with his or her brothers and sisters
C. All four of your grandparents from both sides of the family
D. Your great-grandparents and their neighbors
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Your parent or guardian along with his or her brothers and sisters
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Requirement 7 asks for one family group record listing you and your siblings as the children, and a second form listing your parent or guardian and his or her brothers and sisters as the children of your grandparents (p. 44).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How have microfilming and record indexing worked together to transform genealogical research?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How have microfilming and record indexing worked together to transform genealogical research?
options: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
B. Indexing replaced the need to ever read original birth or census certificates
C. Microfilming automatically translates handwritten foreign records into modern English
D. Family History Centers charge a per-page fee to index private family diaries
choices: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
B. Indexing replaced the need to ever read original birth or census certificates
C. Microfilming automatically translates handwritten foreign records into modern English
D. Family History Centers charge a per-page fee to index private family diaries
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Microfilming preserved over two million rolls of fragile records at institutions like the Family History Library, and record indexing allows researchers to locate specific ancestors across those vast collections in seconds (p. 20).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When discussing your genealogical findings with your counselor for Requirement 9, what is the primary goal?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When discussing your genealogical findings with your counselor for Requirement 9, what is the primary goal?
options: A. Proving that your ancestors were famous historical figures
B. Sharing what you learned about your family and family members through your interviews and record research
C. Memorizing the birth and death dates of every person in a county census
D. Submitting your family's original heirloom documents to a national archive
choices: A. Proving that your ancestors were famous historical figures
B. Sharing what you learned about your family and family members through your interviews and record research
C. Memorizing the birth and death dates of every person in a county census
D. Submitting your family's original heirloom documents to a national archive
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Sharing what you learned about your family and family members through your interviews and record research
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Requirement 9 focuses on reflecting on and discussing what you discovered about your family and individual relatives through your interviews, timelines, records, and charts (p. 58).

pamphlet_excerpts: Terrain Risk Assessment: Steep ravines and loose rock scree require sturdy hiking boots with ankle support.
Wildlife Protection Protocols: Searchers must avoid reaching blindly into rocky crevices where venomous snakes rest.
Weather Monitoring Rules: Rapid temperature drops demand waterproof outer layers packed in personal day packs.
Buddy System Standards: Traveling in pairs prevents isolation during physical injury or sudden navigation failures.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Route Planning: Review topographic contour lines and local park regulations before entering the field.
Step 2 - Equipment Checks: Pack hydration bladders, first aid kits, extra batteries, and weather gear.
Step 3 - Visual Hazard Scan: Scan ground cover and tree branches continuously while walking along the trail.
Step 4 - Incident Logging: Record minor scratches immediately and report any venomous bites to emergency dispatchers.

pamphlet_excerpts: Burial Prohibition Rule: Placing containers beneath disturbed soil violates land manager permits and park regulations.
Surface Camouflage Methods: Conceal containers using loose surface bark, fallen branches, or natural hollow rocks.
Public Property Permissions: Cache placement requires explicit documented authorization from municipal park rangers or landowners.
Cache Removal Responsibilities: Owners must remove containers and archive listings when regular maintenance ceases permanently.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Site Authorization: Obtain written permission from the property administrator before placing any physical container.
Step 2 - Container Selection: Choose durable waterproof ammo cans or sealed gasket boxes with official markings.
Step 3 - Natural Placement: Position the container above ground inside existing dead tree hollows or crevices.
Step 4 - Ethics Verification: Check that retrieval paths cause no vegetation trampling or bank erosion damage.

left_points: (2a) Cache Excavation Ban Policies: Burying caches creates destructive ground disturbance and raises public security concerns regarding buried items. Regulations require every container to rest above the existing mineral soil line.
right_points: (2b) Container Lifecycle and Etiquette: Hiders must monitor moisture seals, replace soggy logbooks, and archive abandoned geocaches responsibly. Searchers must re-hide containers precisely where found without drawing bystander attention.

rows.left: (2a) Why Caches Are Never Buried: Never use artifacts as cache items (p. 54).
rows.right: (2b) Cache Hiding and Maintenance Etiquette: Carry an extra trash bag for trash, leftover and dropped food, and litter left by others. Use established bathrooms when available (p. 54).

rows.left: Cache In Trash Out Practice: Always carry a trash bag with you and practice Cache In Trash Out (CITO) each time you go geocaching (p. 54).
rows.right: (2c) Leave No Trace Principles: Always carry a trash bag with you and practice Cache In Trash Out (CITO) each time you go geocaching (p. 54).

rows.left: Respecting Historic Structures and Artifacts: Observe, but do not touch, cultural or historic structures and artifacts (p. 54).
rows.right: Step 3 - Replace Lifted Rocks Carefully: If you lift a rock to look under it, replace it exactly as you found (p. 54).

pamphlet_excerpts: Satellite Constellation Geometry: Twenty-four active satellites orbit Earth transmitting continuous radio timing signals to receivers.
Trilateration Positioning Methods: Receivers calculate distance from four distinct satellites to establish accurate three-dimensional fixes.
Map Datum Standards: The World Geodetic System 1984 datum provides global standardized coordinate alignment.
Waypoint Management Skills: Users save current location coordinates into memory and edit labels for retrieval.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Explain Concept: Explain satellite trilateration and radio signal timing to patrol members using diagrams.
Step 2 - Demonstrate Function: Demonstrate marking an active waypoint and editing its displayed name and icon.
Step 3 - Guide Practice: Guide the learner through switching coordinate formats to degrees and decimal minutes.
Step 4 - Enable Execution: Observe the Scout independently navigating toward a designated test waypoint coordinate target.

choices: A. By measuring variations in Earth's magnetic field and local barometric air pressure

quiz_item.correct_answer: D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): All GPS satellites transmit their location and current time simultaneously, and the receiver calculates its position by measuring the slight differences in arrival times from 24 to 30 orbiting satellites (p. 11).

pamphlet_excerpts: Magnetic Compass Reliability: Magnetic needles align with Earth magnetic fields without requiring battery electrical power.
Topographic Map Contours: Contour lines reveal elevation changes, steep cliffs, waterways, and impassable physical terrain.
Declination Angle Corrections: Users adjust compass declination to align magnetic north with true map north.
Navigation Redundancy Value: Carrying paper maps prevents wilderness stranding when receiver batteries deplete completely outside.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Map Orientation: Orient the topographic paper map using magnetic north indicated by the compass.
Step 2 - Terrain Correlation: Match visible mountain peaks and stream valleys to contour lines on paper.
Step 3 - Bearing Comparison: Compare electronic GPS bearings against needle headings taken with the baseplate compass.
Step 4 - Route Verification: Plot the final search path on paper before moving toward target coordinates.

B. Because heavy tree cover, narrow canyons, or tall buildings can block satellite reception and GPS units fail without showing terrain obstacles
C. Because GPS satellites are turned off over wilderness areas during the winter months
D. Because a magnetic compass automatically points directly toward plastic geocache containers
choices: A. Because geocaching rules prohibit turning on a GPS unit until you are within 100 feet of the cache
B. Because heavy tree cover, narrow canyons, or tall buildings can block satellite reception and GPS units fail without showing terrain obstacles
C. Because GPS satellites are turned off over wilderness areas during the winter months

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Because heavy tree cover, narrow canyons, or tall buildings can block satellite reception and GPS units fail without showing terrain obstacles

pamphlet_excerpts: Cache Research Phase: Review online descriptions, hint decryptions, container sizes, and recent seeker logs beforehand.
Waypoint Navigation Phase: Follow the receiver directional arrow until distance counts down to twenty feet.
Visual Search Phase: Search natural crevices, hollow stumps, and artificial hangers using observant eyes instead.
Log Signing Phase: Sign the physical paper scroll and reseal container gaskets tightly against moisture.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Research Cache: Read online coordinates, difficulty ratings, cache sizes, and encrypted hints thoroughly beforehand.
Step 2 - Navigate Proximity: Follow the GPS directional arrow until entering the target search zone perimeter.
Step 3 - Scan Environment: Search unusual rock formations, hollow fence posts, and hanging pine branch hooks.
Step 4 - Record Discovery: Sign the paper logbook, replace swag items, and conceal the container securely.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) If a Cache to Eagle® series exists in your council, visit at least three of the locations in the series. Describe the projects that each cache you visit highlights, and explain how the Cache to Eagle® program helps share our Scouting service with the public. (b) Create a Scouting-related Travel Bug® that promotes one of the values of Scouting. Release your Travel Bug into a public geocache and, with your parent or guardian's permission, monitor its progress at www. geocaching. com for 30 days. Keep a log, and share this with your counselor at the end of the 30-day period. (c) Set up and hide a public geocache, following the guidelines in the Geocaching merit badge pamphlet. Before doing so, share with your counselor a three-month maintenance plan for the geocache where you are personally responsible for those three months. After setting up the geocache, with your parent or guardian's permission, follow the logs online for 30 days and share them with your counselor. You must archive the geocache when you are no longer maintaining it. (d) Explain what Cache In Trash Out (CITO) means, and describe how you have practiced CITO at public geocaches or at a CITO event. Then, either create CITO containers to leave at public caches, or host a CITO event for your unit or for the public.

pamphlet_excerpts: Cache to Eagle: Special series caches highlight completed Eagle Scout community leadership service project locations.
Travel Bug Management: Metal tracking tags travel between physical containers fulfilling specific public mission goals.
Container Stewardship Plans: Hiders commit to inspecting containers quarterly, replacing soggy logs, and repairing seals.
Clean In Trash Out: Cache In Trash Out programs remove litter from public parks during searches.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Project Selection: Select one community stewardship option matching troop service goals and local resources.
Step 2 - Stakeholder Coordination: Coordinate with park rangers, council coordinators, or cache owners before beginning work.
Step 3 - Action Execution: Execute the cleanup event, cache placement, or travel bug trackable mission release.
Step 4 - Documentation Review: Document project results and present photographs and maintenance records to your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Thematic Route Planning: Select an engaging educational theme connecting multiple sequential waypoints along safe pathways.
Waypoint Coordinate Averaging: Average coordinates at each station to ensure participants receive accurate navigation targets.
EDGE Method Instruction: Teach navigation by explaining, demonstrating, guiding practice, and enabling independent patrol searches.
Course Safety Boundaries: Establish physical boundary lines and emergency muster checkpoints before releasing youth participants.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Design Route: Map four distinct educational waypoints following a cohesive historic or ecological theme.
Step 2 - Program Waypoints: Enter accurate coordinates and clue descriptions into all youth patrol GPS receivers.
Step 3 - Instruct Participants: Teach receiver screen functions and compass bearing navigation using the EDGE method.
Step 4 - Supervise Hunt: Monitor patrol movements, enforce buddy systems, and conduct an educational game debriefing.

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Cache In Trash Out (CITO) is the practice of always carrying a trash bag while geocaching to pick up litter and leave the outdoor environment cleaner than you found it (p. 54).

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Icons on a cache detail page that show specific characteristics like kid-friendly access or 24-hour availability

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does a GPS receiver calculate its position on Earth?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a GPS receiver calculate its position on Earth?
options: A. By measuring variations in Earth's magnetic field and local barometric air pressure
B. By bouncing a laser beam off cell phone towers within five miles of the trailhead
C. By taking high-resolution photographs of the ground from orbit and matching landmarks
D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
choices: A. By measuring variations in Earth's magnetic field and local barometric air pressure
B. By bouncing a laser beam off cell phone towers within five miles of the trailhead
C. By taking high-resolution photographs of the ground from orbit and matching landmarks
D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): All GPS satellites transmit their location and current time simultaneously, and the receiver calculates its position by measuring the slight differences in arrival times from 24 to 30 orbiting satellites (p. 11).

D. Because a magnetic compass automatically points directly toward plastic geocache containers
choices: A. Because geocaching rules prohibit turning on a GPS unit until you are within 100 feet of the cache
B. Because heavy tree cover, narrow canyons, or tall buildings can block satellite reception and GPS units fail without showing terrain obstacles

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Because heavy tree cover, narrow canyons, or tall buildings can block satellite reception and GPS units fail without showing terrain obstacles
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Heavy tree cover, nearby power lines, tall buildings, and narrow canyons can block or degrade satellite reception, and batteries or electronics can fail, making a map and compass essential (p. 27).

pamphlet_excerpts: Discipline Definition: Planetary geologists investigate crustal materials, mineral compositions, and deep tectonic dynamics.
Rock Outcrop Analysis: Exposed strata formations reveal sedimentary layers through fossil identification and strike measurements.
Uniformitarianism Principle: Present day physical erosion and volcanic eruptions explain ancient stratigraphic sedimentary sequences.
Core Sample Drilling: Deep cylindrical rock cores provide pristine evidence of buried subsurface structural folds.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Field Notebook Setup: Record local outcrop coordinates, weather conditions, and precise bedding strike measurements.
Step 2 - Outcrop Visual Observation: Sketch visible horizontal rock strata while marking color changes and erosional disconformities.
Step 3 - Rock Texture Comparison: Examine grain boundary sorting with a ten power hand lens across specimens.
Step 4 - Modern Process Correlation: Compare river ripple marks on mud bars with ancient lithified sandstone silt.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
quiz_item.question: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
options: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
choices: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Uniformitarianism holds that ongoing geologic processes (magma crystallization, erosion, sedimentation, lithification, and metamorphism) explain the rock structures and stratigraphic record formed over geologic time.

pamphlet_excerpts: Geophysical Exploration: Aeromagnetic surveys and gravity anomaly measurements pinpoint deep hidden metallic ore bodies.
Surface Mining Extraction: Open pit quarries remove overburden rock layers to expose massive copper porphyry.
Froth Flotation Separation: Chemical froth baths separate pulverized copper sulfide minerals from crushed gangue rock.
Petroleum Hydrocarbon Refining: Fractional distillation towers heat crude oil to isolate gasoline, diesel, and bitumen.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Resource Target Selection: Research three distinct economic commodities such as copper ore, petroleum, and aggregate.
Step 2 - Geological Prospecting Mapping: Chart magnetic anomalies and geochemical stream sediment assays indicating concentrated subsurface deposits.
Step 3 - Extraction Method Evaluation: Outline surface quarry excavation steps versus underground room and pillar shaft operations.
Step 4 - Industrial Processing Flowchart: Diagram smelting furnaces or fractional distillation columns separating target minerals from impurities.

pamphlet_excerpts: Standard Map Legend: Letter codes indicate geological age periods and formal formation names across regional sheets.
Rock Classification Symbols: Distinctive patterns differentiate volcanic basalt flows from bedded limestone and foliated gneiss.
Stratigraphic Contact Lines: Solid lines demarcate conformable strata while dashed boundaries represent concealed fault fractures.
Geologic Strike Orientation: Strike and dip symbols display the compass orientation and tilt of beds.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Map Index Orientation: Locate your home county on a state geological survey quadrangle index map.
Step 2 - Stratigraphic Unit Identification: Match outcrop map colors to the explanation column displaying rock formation names.
Step 3 - Major Class Determination: Categorize mapped local bedrock units into igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic lithological classes.
Step 4 - Geological History Deduction: Correlate mapped fault lines and unit ages to reconstruct historical tectonic events.

left_points: Grain Size Cooling Depth: Rock texture, or grain size, provides information about the depth at which the minerals in the magma began to cool, forming igneous rocks (p. 66).
Fine Grained Extrusive Rocks: As an example, if you find a fine-grained igneous rock, you interpret the rock to be an extrusive rock that cooled at or near the surface (p. 66).
Coarse Grained Intrusive Rocks: Coarse-grained igneous rocks are intrusive rocks that cooled over very long periods of time (p. 66).
right_points: Step 1 - Identify Slow Cooling Intrusive Rocks: Coarse-grained igneous rocks are intrusive rocks that cooled over very long periods of time (p. 66).

Step 2 - Trace Uplift and Weathering Exposure: These deep rocks get to the surface when tectonic (mountain-building) forces uplift the area and the material covering the intrusive rock is eroded away by wind (p. 66).
Step 3 - Inspect Rock Color for Minerals: Another important characteristic of igneous rocks is color, which indicates the kinds of rock minerals (p. 66).

options: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust
C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring
D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (b) Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site. (c) Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (d) Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Electricity generation in the United States relies heavily on natural gas, coal, nuclear uranium, hydro, and wind energy. Hydrocarbon extraction requires an organic-rich source rock, porous reservoir rock, and an impermeable structural or stratigraphic trap.
pamphlet_excerpts: Electricity generation in the United States relies heavily on natural gas, coal, nuclear uranium, hydro, and wind energy. Hydrocarbon extraction requires an organic-rich source rock, porous reservoir rock, and an impermeable structural or stratigraphic trap.

sub_requirements.label: (c)
sub_requirements.text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Minerals are naturally occurring, inorganic solids with definite chemical formulas and ordered internal crystalline arrangements. Rocks consist of consolidated mineral aggregates categorized into igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic classes by genetic origin.
pamphlet_excerpts: Minerals are naturally occurring, inorganic solids with definite chemical formulas and ordered internal crystalline arrangements. Rocks consist of consolidated mineral aggregates categorized into igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic classes by genetic origin.

sub_requirements.label: (d)
sub_requirements.text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

children.text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. left_points: (4a) Surface and Sedimentary Dynamics: Sediment particles settle through water columns at rates determined by particle diameter and fluid viscosity according to Stokes law. requirements.description: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (b) Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site. (c) Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (d) Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

pamphlet_excerpts: Specimen Collection Ethics: Take only small representative chips rather than destroying significant structural field outcrops.
Property Permission Protocols: Secure written property owner consent prior to collecting geological samples on private land.
Fragile Microhabitat Protection: Replace overturned rocks promptly to preserve lichen colonies and sensitive subterranean organisms.
Leave No Trace Travel: Walk durable rocky surfaces to prevent trail braiding and rapid slope erosion.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Land Management Review: Contact land managers to confirm collecting regulations and obtain required research permits.
Step 2 - Outcrop Integrity Assessment: Photograph rare geological features rather than dislodging specimens with a rock hammer.
Step 3 - Habitat Preservation Action: Return disturbed rocks to their original positions to protect local soil ecosystems.
Step 4 - Camp and Travel Discipline: Pack out all waste and camp on durable rock slabs when trekking.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
options: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
choices: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Uniformitarianism holds that ongoing geologic processes (magma crystallization, erosion, sedimentation, lithification, and metamorphism) explain the rock structures and stratigraphic record formed over geologic time.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What three stages must all Earth natural resources go through before people can use them in daily life?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What three stages must all Earth natural resources go through before people can use them in daily life?
options: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
B. They must be synthesized in laboratories before being buried in mines
C. They can be pumped or dug directly into finished consumer products without refinement
D. They are gathered exclusively from surface riverbeds without geological exploration
choices: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
B. They must be synthesized in laboratories before being buried in mines
C. They can be pumped or dug directly into finished consumer products without refinement
D. They are gathered exclusively from surface riverbeds without geological exploration
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): All natural resources must follow a three-stage sequence: they must be found (discovered), extracted (removed from Earth), and processed before they can be used (p. 37).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do coarse-grained intrusive igneous rocks that formed deep underground eventually become exposed at Earth's surface?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do coarse-grained intrusive igneous rocks that formed deep underground eventually become exposed at Earth's surface?
options: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust
C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring
D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
choices: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust
C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring
D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Deep intrusive rocks reach Earth's surface when mountain-building tectonic forces uplift the area and wind and water erode away the overlying material (p. 66).

options: A. Deep inside underground volcanic magma tubes
B. Along the shoreline bounded by the levels of high and low tide
C. Floating permanently at the surface of the open mid-ocean far from land
D. Exclusively inside freshwater mountain glaciers
choices: A. Deep inside underground volcanic magma tubes
B. Along the shoreline bounded by the levels of high and low tide
C. Floating permanently at the surface of the open mid-ocean far from land
D. Exclusively inside freshwater mountain glaciers
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Along the shoreline bounded by the levels of high and low tide
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Littoral animals live along the shoreline zone bounded by the levels of high and low tide, whereas benthic organisms live on the seafloor (p. 70).

options: A. Cold rainwater freezing inside surface mud cracks during winter
B. Wind blowing desert sand grains across flat limestone plateaus
C. Very hot steam and hydrothermal solutions moving through existing rock and altering its minerals
D. Ocean waves polishing pebbles along a sandy beach
choices: A. Cold rainwater freezing inside surface mud cracks during winter
B. Wind blowing desert sand grains across flat limestone plateaus
C. Very hot steam and hydrothermal solutions moving through existing rock and altering its minerals

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Very hot steam and hydrothermal solutions moving through existing rock and altering its minerals
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Hydrothermal solutions, which are very hot steam and mineral-rich fluids often associated with metamorphic processes, penetrate surrounding rocks to form many of the world's ore deposits (p. 68).

requirements.description: Discuss safety on the golf course. Show that you know first aid for injuries or illnesses that could occur while golfing, including lightning, heat reactions, sunburn, dehydration, blisters, animal or bug bites, poison ivy exposure, sprains, and strains.
requirements.workbook_visual_caption: Scouts and counselor demonstrate Golf Requirement 1 field procedures and safety checks.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Golfers must immediately clear open fairways and seek grounded lightning shelters upon hearing severe weather detection sirens. Treatment for heat illness or ankle sprains requires immediate shade, hydration, and elevation before resuming play.
socratic_questions: Why does holding a graphite or steel golf club during an incoming storm drastically heighten strike risks?
How do early symptoms of dehydration impair a golfer's physical balance and shot execution?
What immediate steps should your group take if a stray golf ball strikes an adjacent player?

requirements.lead_text: Complete ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Traditional Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the USGA Rules of Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the three categories of golf etiquette. (b) Demonstrate that you understand the definitions of golf terms. (c) Show that you understand the Rules of Amateur Status. (2) Tell about your understanding of the World Handicap System. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the early history of golf. (b) Describe golf's early years in the United States. (c) Tell about the accomplishments of a top golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) The proper grip, stance, posture, and key fundamentals of a good swing (b) Driver played from a tee (c) The fairway wood shot (d) The long iron shot (e) The short iron shot (f) The approach, chip-and-run, and pitch shots (g) A recovery shot from a bunker or heavy rough (h) A sound putting stroke (6) Play a minimum of two nine-hole rounds or one 18-hole round of golf with another golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the Rules of Golf. (b) Practice good golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow golfers, committee, sponsor, and gallery. (7) Find out about three careers related to traditional golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you. (b) Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you.
