pamphlet_excerpts: Deep Water Entry: Jump feet first into water over head depth and level off smoothly.
Continuous Lap Distance: Swim one hundred yards continuously using strong forward arm strokes without resting.
Stroke Mechanics Variety: Complete seventy five yards using an assertive forward stroke and twenty five breaststroke.
Resting Float Recovery: Maintain an effortless resting back float with minimal arm or leg movement.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Surface Plunge: Leap cleanly into deep water feet first and level off without thrashing.
Step 2 - Stroke Execution: Propel forward seventy five yards using strong side or steady crawl strokes.
Step 3 - Form Transition: Switch stroke directly into twenty five yards of restful orthodox breaststroke technique.
Step 4 - Buoyant Rest: Roll backward into an motionless resting float while controlling regular breathing rhythm.

pamphlet_excerpts: Centerboard Hydrodynamic Lift: Lowered underwater foils counteract sideways leeway drift created by aerodynamic sail force.
Rudder Directional Steering: Pivoting underwater blades redirect stern water flow to pivot the vessel bow.
Standing Rigging Support: Wire stays and shrouds stabilize aluminum masts against tremendous aerodynamic sail strain.
Running Rigging Adjustment: Halyards hoist sail corners while mainsheets trim boom angles against the wind.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Hull Inspection: Examine the fiberglass hull, transom fittings, and cockpit self bailers for structural damage.
Step 2 - Foil Installation: Insert the centerboard or secure the daggerboard within the reinforced keel trunk.
Step 3 - Rudder Attachment: Mount pintles securely into gudgeons and lock the safety retaining clip down.
Step 4 - Spar Rigging: Secure shrouds and forestay before stepping the mast into the mast step.

B. The forestay wire attached from the bow to the front of the mast
C. The outhaul line used to pull the clew of the mainsail toward the end of the boom
D. The transom board located across the stern of the hull
choices: A. The centerboard or dagger board lowered through the trunk into the water

quiz_item.correct_answer: A. The centerboard or dagger board lowered through the trunk into the water
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The centerboard or dagger board extends below the hull to provide lateral resistance that counteracts the sideways push of the wind, preventing leeway when sailing upwind (p. 18).

(b) Explain the rules of the road in general and any specific rules or laws that apply to your area or state. (c) Explain how water conditions, the hazards of weather, and heavy winds can affect both safety and performance in sailing. (d) Discuss the warning signs of inclement weather and what to do should heavy winds develop or a storm approach. (e) Prepare a typical float plan. (f) Discuss the proper clothing, footwear, and personal gear required for small-boat sailing in warm weather and in cool weather. Explain how choosing the proper clothing, footwear, and personal gear will help keep you comfortable and safe while sailing.

pamphlet_excerpts: Float Plan Dispatch: Leave written routes, crew rosters, and return times with responsible shore contacts.
Right Of Way: Stand on vessels maintain steady course while give way vessels alter heading.
Thermal Clothing Selection: Layer synthetic fleece and windproof shells while avoiding heat draining wet cotton fabrics.
Squall Visual Indicators: Dark towering cumulonimbus clouds signal sudden violent gusts and rapid wind shifts.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Document Creation: Draft a float plan detailing vessel description, intended course, and emergency contact numbers.
Step 2 - Barometer Monitoring: Check local marine weather broadcasts for squall warnings and falling atmospheric barometric trends.
Step 3 - Gear Selection: Don closed toe non marking deck shoes and layered moisture wicking synthetic apparel.
Step 4 - Navigation Briefing: Review port and starboard tack right of way rules before leaving the marina.
gear_checklist: U.S. Coast Guard-approved Type III Personal Flotation Device (PFD) properly fitted and buckled
Waterfront rescue throw bag (50 ft floating polypropylene line), reach pole, and safety whistle
BSA Safe Swim Defense / Safety Afloat buddy tags and watercraft inspection checklist
Bilge pump or bailer, spare paddle/oar, painter lines, and dry bag with thermal layer

left_points: (4a) Safety Afloat Nine Points: Safety Afloat establishes mandatory supervision, physical fitness standards, and designated craft boundaries. Qualified adult leaders verify weather conditions and maintain active buddy pairs throughout the float.

(4b) Maritime Navigation Rules Road: Port tack vessels yield to starboard tack vessels, and windward vessels give way to leeward craft. Overtaking vessels must stay clear of overtaken craft regardless of sail trim configurations.

(4c) Water And Wind Hazards: High winds increase heeling forces, requiring crew weight shifts and rapid sheet easing to prevent capsizes. Choppy wave conditions induce leeway drift, reduce forward boat speed, and swamp low freeboard hulls.
right_points: (4d) Inclement Weather Response Tactics: Sudden temperature drops, shifting winds, and darkening clouds indicate incoming frontal storms. Skippers should drop sails immediately, secure loose gear, and paddle toward safe harbor shelters.

(4e) Float Plan Route Preparation: A written float plan documents boat hull markings, crew identities, intended waypoints, and expected return times. Shoreside monitors use this vital record to direct rescue authorities if boats become overdue.

(4f) Nautical Personal Protective Gear: Proper gear includes non skid sailing shoes, polarized sunglasses with safety retainers, and snug thermal apparel. Wet suits or dry suits trap insulating layers against cold spray to preserve core warmth.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: According to the navigation rules of the road, what happens when two sailboats approach each other on opposite tacks?
quiz_item.question: According to the navigation rules of the road, what happens when two sailboats approach each other on opposite tacks?
options: A. Both boats must immediately drop their sails and wait for the other to pass
B. The boat on the starboard tack must give way and steer behind the port-tack boat
C. Whichever boat has the larger mainsail automatically holds the right-of-way
D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
choices: A. Both boats must immediately drop their sails and wait for the other to pass
B. The boat on the starboard tack must give way and steer behind the port-tack boat
C. Whichever boat has the larger mainsail automatically holds the right-of-way
D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When two sailboats approach on opposite tacks, the vessel on the port tack (wind coming over the port side) is the give-way vessel and must steer clear of the vessel on the starboard tack (p. 22).

pamphlet_excerpts: Masthead Fly Observation: Pivoting wind vanes mounted at mastheads indicate instantaneous apparent wind direction overhead.
Surface Water Ripples: Dark patches of ripples moving across calm water reveal approaching fresh wind gusts.
Facial Sensory Perception: Turning face directly into the breeze reveals accurate wind bearing across both cheeks.
Shrouded Sail Telltales: Streaming yarn ribbons taped on sail fabric indicate laminar air attachment or stall.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Shoreline Observation: Check shoreline flags and wave direction to determine general prevailing true wind bearing.
Step 2 - Masthead Alignment: Look directly upward at the masthead vane to confirm localized surface wind angles.
Step 3 - Sail Ribbon Check: Observe windward and leeward jib telltales while slowly heading into the breeze.
Step 4 - Course Plotting: Identify the no sail zone boundaries before releasing shore dock mooring lines.

quiz_item.question: How can a sailor accurately identify the wind direction before leaving the dock or beach?
options: A. Looking only at the direction the underwater weeds are leaning near the dock pilings
B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
C. Checking which way the rudder blade floats when the boat is tied tightly to a slip
D. Waiting until the sails are fully sheeted in at the dock to see which way the boat capsizes
choices: A. Looking only at the direction the underwater weeds are leaning near the dock pilings
B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
C. Checking which way the rudder blade floats when the boat is tied tightly to a slip
D. Waiting until the sails are fully sheeted in at the dock to see which way the boat capsizes
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Ripples and darker patches of water (cat's-paws), onshore flags, mooring boats pointing into the breeze, and masthead wind indicators all reveal wind direction before you launch (p. 26).

requirements.lead_text: Following the Scouting America Safety Afloat plan, show that you and a buddy can sail a boat properly. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Following the Scouting America Safety Afloat plan, show that you and a buddy can sail a boat properly. Do the following: (a) Prepare a boat for sailing, including a safety inspection. (b) Get underway from a dock, mooring, or beach. (c) Properly set sails for a round-trip course approved by your counselor that will include running, beating, and reaching, the basic points of sail. While sailing, demonstrate good helmsmanship skills. (d) Change direction by tacking; change direction by jibing. (e) Demonstrate getting out of irons. (f) Demonstrate the safety position. (g) Demonstrate capsize procedures and the rescue of a person overboard. Note: Capsize procedures should be conducted under the close supervision of the counselor. A rescue boat should be standing by to assist, if necessary, and to tow the capsized craft to shore. Self-bailing boats are acceptable for this requirement. Extreme care should be taken to avoid personal injury and damage to the boat or equipment. (h) Demonstrate the procedure to take after running aground. (i) Accept a single line or side tow and maneuver the craft being towed safely for 20 boat lengths. (j) Upon returning to the dock, mooring, or beach, properly secure all equipment, furl or stow sails, and prepare the craft for unattended docking or beaching overnight or longer.

pamphlet_excerpts: Controlled Tack Rotation: Push the tiller smoothly toward the sail to bring the bow through wind.
Controlled Jibe Sweep: Pull the tiller away from sail while centering the boom across centerline.
Capsize Daggerboard Leverage: Stand on the exposed daggerboard foil to lever the submerged mast upright.
Overboard Rescue Approach: Circle back on a close reach to stop boat momentum beside the victim.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Hull Inspection: Inspect drain plugs, check standing wire rigging, and confirm centerboard deployment functionality.
Step 2 - Departure Clearance: Cast off dock lines while pushing the bow toward a clear reach angle.
Step 3 - Course Execution: Steer an approved course demonstrating close hauled beating, beam reaching, and broad running.
Step 4 - Mooring Securing: Luff sails completely into the wind while easing sheets to stop beside dock.

left_points: (6a) Pre-Sail Rigging Safety Inspection: Rigging inspection confirms hull integrity, rudder pin retention, and halyard shackle locks before launch. Crew members secure drain plugs tightly to prevent catastrophic cockpit flooding while underway.

(6b) Dock Departure Underway Maneuvers: Departing requires pushing the bow onto a reach before trimming sheets to gather forward steerage. Helmsmen coordinate line release so wind pushes the hull cleanly into open navigation channels.

(6c) Course Sail Trim Points: Beating demands tight sail trim and lowered foils, while reaching eases sails halfway out. When running before the wind, centerboards are raised halfway to reduce underwater drag and leeway friction.
right_points: (6f) Heaving To Safety Position: The safety position arrests forward movement by backing the jib and lashing the helm down. The mainsail feathers harmlessly, holding the boat stable in open water for crew rest or reefing.

(6g) Capsize And Overboard Rescue: During capsizes, crew members stay with the hull, lower sails, and apply body weight on the centerboard. Rescuing an overboard sailor requires circling downwind and luffing alongside on a close reach.

(6h) Aground Vessel Recovery Actions: Running aground requires immediate sail easing to eliminate heeling and forward drive against shoals. Crew members raise the centerboard, shift weight aft, and use paddles to push into deeper water.

quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): When a boat is stuck in irons (pointed directly into the no-sail zone with zero headway), backing the jib or boom to one side while positioning the tiller lets the wind push the bow off the wind onto a tack (p. 31).

requirements.description: Following the Scouting America Safety Afloat plan, show that you and a buddy can sail a boat properly. Do the following: (a) Prepare a boat for sailing, including a safety inspection. (b) Get underway from a dock, mooring, or beach. (c) Properly set sails for a round-trip course approved by your counselor that will include running, beating, and reaching, the basic points of sail. While sailing, demonstrate good helmsmanship skills. (d) Change direction by tacking; change direction by jibing. (e) Demonstrate getting out of irons. (f) Demonstrate the safety position. (g) Demonstrate capsize procedures and the rescue of a person overboard. Note: Capsize procedures should be conducted under the close supervision of the counselor. A rescue boat should be standing by to assist, if necessary, and to tow the capsized craft to shore. Self-bailing boats are acceptable for this requirement. Extreme care should be taken to avoid personal injury and damage to the boat or equipment. (h) Demonstrate the procedure to take after running aground. (i) Accept a single line or side tow and maneuver the craft being towed safely for 20 boat lengths. (j) Upon returning to the dock, mooring, or beach, properly secure all equipment, furl or stow sails, and prepare the craft for unattended docking or beaching overnight or longer.

pamphlet_excerpts: Bowline Non Slip Loop: Form an unshakeable fixed eye loop that will not slip under load.
Cleat Hitch Security: Wrap a clean locking hitch around deck cleats without jamming redundant hitches.
Dacron Halyard Strength: Low stretch polyester fibers maintain steady sail shape without stretching under hoist tension.
Faking Down Preparedness: Flake sheets in overlapping figure eight patterns for rapid, jam free line running.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Knot Execution: Tie a secure bowline and figure eight stopper knot in specified line ends.
Step 2 - Cleat Fastening: Wrap a round turn, figure eight crosses, and reverse locking half hitch on cleats.
Step 3 - Line Throwing: Coil half the line in each hand and heave smoothly toward target crew.
Step 4 - Cordage Inspection: Evaluate nylon versus polyester lines for stretch, sun rot, and core abrasion damage.

pamphlet_excerpts: Freshwater Hardware Rinse: Wash salt crystals off stainless blocks and anodized aluminum spars to stop corrosion.
Fiberglass Gelcoat Protection: Apply marine paste wax on topsides to shield gelcoat against destructive solar rays.
Sail Cleaning Mildew: Wash sailcloth with mild freshwater detergent and dry completely before winterizing inside bags.
Winter Storage Elevation: Support stored boat hulls on shaped bunks off the ground under ventilated covers.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Hardware Wash: Flush salt crystals from cam cleats, blocks, and mast tangs using clean freshwater.
Step 2 - Hull Inspection: Check fiberglass gelcoat surfaces for stress cracks, gouges, and loose deck joint rivets.
Step 3 - Sail Inspection: Examine sail stitching, bolt ropes, and batten pockets for torn seams or chafe.
Step 4 - Winter Layup: Drain cockpit bilges and position hulls onto cradles beneath breathable canvas winter tarps.

options: A. Store your PFD under the foredeck, stand on the gunwale during a jibe, and swim away from the hull if the boat capsizes.
B. Tie the mainsheet in a hard knot to the cleat so your hands are free, and dive under the sail if the boat turtles.
C. Always wear a properly fitted USCG-approved PFD, watch for the boom swinging across the cockpit during tacks and especially jibes, and stay with the floating sailboat if it capsizes.

choices: A. Store your PFD under the foredeck, stand on the gunwale during a jibe, and swim away from the hull if the boat capsizes.
B. Tie the mainsheet in a hard knot to the cleat so your hands are free, and dive under the sail if the boat turtles.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Always wear a properly fitted USCG-approved PFD, watch for the boom swinging across the cockpit during tacks and especially jibes, and stay with the floating sailboat if it capsizes.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Sailing safety requires wearing a USCG-approved PFD at all times, keeping heads low and controlling the mainsheet when the boom crosses during tacks and jibes, and staying with a capsized hull.

options: A. The centerboard or dagger board lowered through the trunk into the water
B. The forestay wire attached from the bow to the front of the mast
C. The outhaul line used to pull the clew of the mainsail toward the end of the boom
D. The transom board located across the stern of the hull
choices: A. The centerboard or dagger board lowered through the trunk into the water
B. The forestay wire attached from the bow to the front of the mast
C. The outhaul line used to pull the clew of the mainsail toward the end of the boom

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. The centerboard or dagger board lowered through the trunk into the water
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The centerboard or dagger board extends below the hull to provide lateral resistance that counteracts the sideways push of the wind, preventing leeway when sailing upwind (p. 18).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the navigation rules of the road, what happens when two sailboats approach each other on opposite tacks?
options: A. Both boats must immediately drop their sails and wait for the other to pass
B. The boat on the starboard tack must give way and steer behind the port-tack boat
C. Whichever boat has the larger mainsail automatically holds the right-of-way
D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
choices: A. Both boats must immediately drop their sails and wait for the other to pass
B. The boat on the starboard tack must give way and steer behind the port-tack boat
C. Whichever boat has the larger mainsail automatically holds the right-of-way
D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When two sailboats approach on opposite tacks, the vessel on the port tack (wind coming over the port side) is the give-way vessel and must steer clear of the vessel on the starboard tack (p. 22).

B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
C. Checking which way the rudder blade floats when the boat is tied tightly to a slip

choices: A. Looking only at the direction the underwater weeds are leaning near the dock pilings
B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales

D. Waiting until the sails are fully sheeted in at the dock to see which way the boat capsizes
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Ripples and darker patches of water (cat's-paws), onshore flags, mooring boats pointing into the breeze, and masthead wind indicators all reveal wind direction before you launch (p. 26).

options: A. Pulling the mainsheet and jib sheet as tight as possible while keeping the rudder centered
B. Dropping the anchor immediately and waiting for the wind direction to shift 90 degrees
C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
D. Raising the centerboard completely out of the trunk and paddling backward toward the dock
choices: A. Pulling the mainsheet and jib sheet as tight as possible while keeping the rudder centered
B. Dropping the anchor immediately and waiting for the wind direction to shift 90 degrees
C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
D. Raising the centerboard completely out of the trunk and paddling backward toward the dock
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): When a boat is stuck in irons (pointed directly into the no-sail zone with zero headway), backing the jib or boom to one side while positioning the tiller lets the wind push the bow off the wind onto a tack (p. 31).

pamphlet_excerpts: Green Circle: Green circles designate easier beginner slopes with wide contours and gentle gradients.
Blue Square: Blue squares indicate more difficult intermediate terrain with moderate pitches and moguls.
Black Diamond: Black diamonds denote most difficult trails featuring steep pitches, narrow chutes, and obstacles.
Double Diamond: Double black diamonds identify expert terrain containing extreme cliff bands and hazards.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Map Consultation: Review the resort trail map before riding lifts to identify appropriate routes.
Step 2 - Signboard Verification: Match the trail head marker shape to personal technical competence before dropping.
Step 3 - Boundary Respect: Obey orange rope closures denoting ungroomed terrain, thin cover, or avalanche closures.
Step 4 - Junction Decision: Choose lower difficulty bypass routes whenever approaching intersections with double black diamonds.

Core Stability: Planks strengthen abdominal muscles to maintain proper balance over shifting snow conditions.
Cardiovascular Stamina: Aerobic conditioning delays muscular exhaustion that causes late afternoon downhill ski accidents.
Dynamic Flexibility: Leg swings and hamstring stretches protect knees and hips from abrupt torque.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Warmup Routine: Perform five minutes of light jumping jacks to elevate core body temperature.
Step 2 - Quadriceps Loading: Hold a ninety degree wall sit for sixty seconds to develop leg endurance.
Step 3 - Balance Training: Practice single leg squats on a balance pad to strengthen ankle stabilizers.
Step 4 - Dynamic Stretching: Complete deep lunges and torso rotations to improve hip mobility before skiing.

pamphlet_excerpts: Base Layer: Synthetic or merino wool base layers pull perspiration away from cold skin.
Insulation Layer: Fleece or down mid-layers trap warm air without restricting downhill athletic motion.
Outer Shell: Waterproof breathable outer jackets block biting wind and repel freezing mountain precipitation.
Head Protection: Certified snow helmets retain head warmth while shielding skulls from high-speed impacts.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Base Layering: Put on moisture wicking polyester thermal underwear against the bare dry skin.
Step 2 - Thermal Stacking: Add a fleece pullover to trap body warmth around the vital organs.
Step 3 - Weather Shelling: Zip up a windproof breathable jacket over pants covering boot tops completely.
Step 4 - Extremity Coverage: Secure waterproof insulated mittens, neck gaiter, helmet, and anti-fog dual-pane goggles snugly.

pamphlet_excerpts: Downhill Right: Downhill skiers have the right of way because they cannot see behind.
Safe Stopping: Avoid stopping in narrow trails or where you are invisible from above.
Park Etiquette: Look before you leap to ensure landing zones are clear of fallen riders.
Avalanche Awareness: Carrying a transceiver, shovel, and probe is mandatory in snowy backcountry terrain.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Control Maintenance: Ski at controlled speeds allowing immediate stops to avoid obstacles and people.
Step 2 - Lookout Verification: Look uphill and yield to oncoming skiers whenever merging onto a trail.
Step 3 - Park Progression: Inspect all terrain park jumps and rails before attempting any aerial maneuvers.
Step 4 - Beacon Check: Test avalanche beacon transmit and receive functions before entering any ungroomed gates.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Downhill (Alpine) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate each of the required skills. (1) Show how to wax and maintain your skis and use/maintain your release bindings. Explain the international DIN standard and what it means to skiers. (2) Explain the American Teaching System and a basic snowskiing progression. (3) Discuss the different types of Alpine skis. Demonstrate two ways to carry skis and poles safely and easily. (4) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (5) On a gentle slope, demonstrate some of the beginning maneuvers learned in skiing. Include the straight run, gliding wedge, wedge stop, sidestep, and herringbone maneuvers. (6) On slightly steeper terrain, show linked wedge turns. (7) On a moderate slope, demonstrate five to 10 christies. (8) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (9) Demonstrate the ability to ski in varied conditions, including changes in pitch and snow conditions. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (10) Name the major ski organizations in the United States and explain their functions. (b) Option B, Cross-Country (Nordic) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show your ability to select, use, and maintain equipment for cross-country skiing in safety and comfort. (2) Explain the reasons for common rules, including no walking on ski trails, one-way ski direction, no pets, and no skiing on snowmobile trails. (3) Discuss classic, skating, touring, and telemark skis. (4) Discuss the basic principles of waxing for cross-country ski touring. (5) Discuss the differences between cross-country, backcountry/ski touring, ski mountaineering, and downhill/telemark skiing. (6) List the items you would take on a one-day ski tour. (7) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass. (8) On a gentle, packed slope, show some basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the straight run, traverse, side slip, step turn, wedge stop, and wedge turn maneuvers. (9) On a cross-country trail, demonstrate effective propulsion by showing proper weight transfer from ski to ski, pole timing, rhythm, flow, and glide. (10) Demonstrate your ability, on a 4-mile tour, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive skiers may complete a 1-mile tour with prior approval from their counselor. (11) Demonstrate several methods of dealing with steep hills or difficult conditions. Include traverses and kick turns going uphill and downhill, sidesteps, and pole drag. (c) Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions. (d) Option D, Snowshoeing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name the parts of a snowshoe. (2) Explain how to choose the correct size of snowshoe. (3) Describe the different types of snowshoes and their specialized uses. Discuss factors to consider when choosing a snowshoe. (4) Explain how to properly care for and maintain snowshoes. (5) List the items you would take on a one-day snowshoe hike. (6) Describe areas that are best for snowshoeing. Discuss some advantages and dangers of backcountry snowshoeing. (7) Discuss the benefits of snowshoeing. (8) Demonstrate the most efficient ways to break trail, climb uphill, travel downhill, and traverse a slope. (9) Demonstrate your ability, on a 2-mile snowshoe hike, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive snowshoers may complete a 1-mile hike with prior approval from their counselor. (10) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Downhill (Alpine) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate each of the required skills. (1) Show how to wax and maintain your skis and use/maintain your release bindings. Explain the international DIN standard and what it means to skiers. (2) Explain the American Teaching System and a basic snowskiing progression. (3) Discuss the different types of Alpine skis. Demonstrate two ways to carry skis and poles safely and easily. (4) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (5) On a gentle slope, demonstrate some of the beginning maneuvers learned in skiing. Include the straight run, gliding wedge, wedge stop, sidestep, and herringbone maneuvers. (6) On slightly steeper terrain, show linked wedge turns. (7) On a moderate slope, demonstrate five to 10 christies. (8) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (9) Demonstrate the ability to ski in varied conditions, including changes in pitch and snow conditions. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (10) Name the major ski organizations in the United States and explain their functions.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Alpine skiing focuses on dynamic balance, rotary motion, pressure control, and edging skills on groomed trails. Skiers master wedge christies, parallel turns, and controlled hockey stops across progressively steeper terrain.
pamphlet_excerpts: Alpine skiing focuses on dynamic balance, rotary motion, pressure control, and edging skills on groomed trails. Skiers master wedge christies, parallel turns, and controlled hockey stops across progressively steeper terrain.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Cross-Country (Nordic) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show your ability to select, use, and maintain equipment for cross-country skiing in safety and comfort. (2) Explain the reasons for common rules, including no walking on ski trails, one-way ski direction, no pets, and no skiing on snowmobile trails. (3) Discuss classic, skating, touring, and telemark skis. (4) Discuss the basic principles of waxing for cross-country ski touring. (5) Discuss the differences between cross-country, backcountry/ski touring, ski mountaineering, and downhill/telemark skiing. (6) List the items you would take on a one-day ski tour. (7) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass. (8) On a gentle, packed slope, show some basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the straight run, traverse, side slip, step turn, wedge stop, and wedge turn maneuvers. (9) On a cross-country trail, demonstrate effective propulsion by showing proper weight transfer from ski to ski, pole timing, rhythm, flow, and glide. (10) Demonstrate your ability, on a 4-mile tour, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive skiers may complete a 1-mile tour with prior approval from their counselor. (11) Demonstrate several methods of dealing with steep hills or difficult conditions. Include traverses and kick turns going uphill and downhill, sidesteps, and pole drag.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Cross-Country (Nordic) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show your ability to select, use, and maintain equipment for cross-country skiing in safety and comfort. (2) Explain the reasons for common rules, including no walking on ski trails, one-way ski direction, no pets, and no skiing on snowmobile trails. (3) Discuss classic, skating, touring, and telemark skis. (4) Discuss the basic principles of waxing for cross-country ski touring. (5) Discuss the differences between cross-country, backcountry/ski touring, ski mountaineering, and downhill/telemark skiing. (6) List the items you would take on a one-day ski tour. (7) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass. (8) On a gentle, packed slope, show some basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the straight run, traverse, side slip, step turn, wedge stop, and wedge turn maneuvers. (9) On a cross-country trail, demonstrate effective propulsion by showing proper weight transfer from ski to ski, pole timing, rhythm, flow, and glide. (10) Demonstrate your ability, on a 4-mile tour, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive skiers may complete a 1-mile tour with prior approval from their counselor. (11) Demonstrate several methods of dealing with steep hills or difficult conditions. Include traverses and kick turns going uphill and downhill, sidesteps, and pole drag.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Nordic skiing incorporates diagonal strides, kick-and-glide mechanics, and uphill herringbone maneuvers across rolling winter landscapes. Equipment utilizes free-heel bindings and specialized wax or fishscale grip patterns to propel the skier.

sub_requirements.label: (c)
sub_requirements.text: Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions.

pamphlet_excerpts: Alpine Edge: Angling ski edges into the snowpack allows controlled turning and stopping power.
Nordic Stride: Diagonal stride combines opposite arm and leg kicks for efficient flatland propulsion.
Snowboard Carve: Shifting weight between heel and toe edges initiates fluid carving across slopes.
Snowshoe Grip: Steel crampons beneath the snowshoe deck provide traction while climbing frozen ascents.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Gear Fitting: Adjust bindings and boot closures to ensure secure attachment without painful pinching.
Step 2 - Stance Centering: Flex knees and ankles slightly forward to maintain a centered athletic posture.
Step 3 - Edge Engagement: Apply subtle lateral pressure to roll edges into the snow for turning.
Step 4 - Controlled Deceleration: Execute a wedge, hockey stop, or toe edge slide to stop cleanly.

left_points: (7a) Downhill Alpine Skiing Techniques: Alpine skiing focuses on dynamic balance, rotary motion, pressure control, and edging skills on groomed trails. Skiers master wedge christies, parallel turns, and controlled hockey stops across progressively steeper terrain.

(7b) Cross Country Nordic Techniques: Nordic skiing incorporates diagonal strides, kick-and-glide mechanics, and uphill herringbone maneuvers across rolling winter landscapes. Equipment utilizes free-heel bindings and specialized wax or fishscale grip patterns to propel the skier.
right_points: (7c) Snowboarding Fundamentals and Carving: Snowboarding requires lateral balance, rotational body movements, and precise transitions between heel-side and toe-side edges. Riders learn safe falls, skidded traverses, and linked carved turns down novice and intermediate trails.

(7d) Snowshoeing Wilderness Navigation Mechanics: Snowshoeing distributes body weight over a broader surface area to achieve flotation over deep unconsolidated snow. Users learn proper stride width, heel-lift ascents, step-turn maneuvers, and safe pole plant coordination.

rows.left: (7a) Downhill Alpine Skiing Techniques: All-mountain skis come in a variety of flexes and side cuts (p. 37).
rows.right: (7c) Snowboarding Control and Maneuvers: They generally have a stiff flex that can make turning more difficult, but that makes the ski more stable at higher speeds (p. 37).

rows.left: (7b) Cross-Country Nordic Skiing Skills: Racing skis are designed for high speeds and hard snow (p. 37).
rows.right: (7d) Snowshoeing Equipment and Backcountry Travel: Racing skis are specialized for turning around gates, and the side cut determines how wide a turn the skis can make (p. 37).

rows.left: Stiff Flex High-Speed Stability: They generally have a stiff flex that can make turning more difficult, but that makes the ski more stable at higher speeds (p. 37).
rows.right: Step 3 - Use Twin-Tips for Parks: Twin-tip skis are turned up at the tip and the tail and are designed for performing on jumps, rails, and half-pipes (p. 37).

requirements.description: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Downhill (Alpine) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate each of the required skills. (1) Show how to wax and maintain your skis and use/maintain your release bindings. Explain the international DIN standard and what it means to skiers. (2) Explain the American Teaching System and a basic snowskiing progression. (3) Discuss the different types of Alpine skis. Demonstrate two ways to carry skis and poles safely and easily. (4) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (5) On a gentle slope, demonstrate some of the beginning maneuvers learned in skiing. Include the straight run, gliding wedge, wedge stop, sidestep, and herringbone maneuvers. (6) On slightly steeper terrain, show linked wedge turns. (7) On a moderate slope, demonstrate five to 10 christies. (8) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (9) Demonstrate the ability to ski in varied conditions, including changes in pitch and snow conditions. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (10) Name the major ski organizations in the United States and explain their functions. (b) Option B, Cross-Country (Nordic) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show your ability to select, use, and maintain equipment for cross-country skiing in safety and comfort. (2) Explain the reasons for common rules, including no walking on ski trails, one-way ski direction, no pets, and no skiing on snowmobile trails. (3) Discuss classic, skating, touring, and telemark skis. (4) Discuss the basic principles of waxing for cross-country ski touring. (5) Discuss the differences between cross-country, backcountry/ski touring, ski mountaineering, and downhill/telemark skiing. (6) List the items you would take on a one-day ski tour. (7) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass. (8) On a gentle, packed slope, show some basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the straight run, traverse, side slip, step turn, wedge stop, and wedge turn maneuvers. (9) On a cross-country trail, demonstrate effective propulsion by showing proper weight transfer from ski to ski, pole timing, rhythm, flow, and glide. (10) Demonstrate your ability, on a 4-mile tour, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive skiers may complete a 1-mile tour with prior approval from their counselor. (11) Demonstrate several methods of dealing with steep hills or difficult conditions. Include traverses and kick turns going uphill and downhill, sidesteps, and pole drag. (c) Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions. (d) Option D, Snowshoeing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name the parts of a snowshoe. (2) Explain how to choose the correct size of snowshoe. (3) Describe the different types of snowshoes and their specialized uses. Discuss factors to consider when choosing a snowshoe. (4) Explain how to properly care for and maintain snowshoes. (5) List the items you would take on a one-day snowshoe hike. (6) Describe areas that are best for snowshoeing. Discuss some advantages and dangers of backcountry snowshoeing. (7) Discuss the benefits of snowshoeing. (8) Demonstrate the most efficient ways to break trail, climb uphill, travel downhill, and traverse a slope. (9) Demonstrate your ability, on a 2-mile snowshoe hike, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive snowshoers may complete a 1-mile hike with prior approval from their counselor. (10) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: While skiing down an intermediate alpine trail, you approach a slower snowboarder ahead of you who suddenly begins a wide turn across the run. Under the Alpine Responsibility Code, who has the right-of-way and what must you do?
options: A. Shout 'On your left!' and pass at high speed since uphill skiers have momentum.
B. The downhill rider ahead always has the right-of-way; you must adjust your speed and steer clear to avoid them regardless of their turn.
C. Stop in the middle of a blind rollover just above the snowboarder and wait.
D. Cut sharply across the tips of the snowboarder's board to claim the center line of the groomer.
choices: A. Shout 'On your left!' and pass at high speed since uphill skiers have momentum.
B. The downhill rider ahead always has the right-of-way; you must adjust your speed and steer clear to avoid them regardless of their turn.
C. Stop in the middle of a blind rollover just above the snowboarder and wait.
D. Cut sharply across the tips of the snowboarder's board to claim the center line of the groomer.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. The downhill rider ahead always has the right-of-way; you must adjust your speed and steer clear to avoid them regardless of their turn.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Under Your Responsibility Code in the Snow Sports Merit Badge Pamphlet, downhill skiers/riders cannot see behind them, so uphill traffic bears full responsibility for avoiding collisions and must never stop where obstructed from above.

options: A. Send a group member to the bottom of the nearest lift to inform the lift operator
B. Wave your ski poles toward the nearest chairlift tower
C. Carry the injured skier down to the base lodge first-aid station
D. Wait at the trail merge until a roving patroller passes by
choices: A. Send a group member to the bottom of the nearest lift to inform the lift operator
B. Wave your ski poles toward the nearest chairlift tower

pamphlet_excerpts: Weathering Process: Physical fracturing and chemical weathering convert parent rock material into microscopic mineral grains.
Organic Humus: Decomposed biological tissue stabilizes aggregate structure and increases moisture holding capacity across topsoil.
Soil Texture Classes: Proportions of sand, silt, and clay establish critical drainage and aeration properties.
Primary Nutrients: Nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium provide chemical fuel for vigorous plant cell development.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Core Extraction: Collect vertical soil core samples using a stainless tube sampler across representative terrain.
Step 2 - Ribbon Assessment: Moisten fine aggregate between thumb and forefinger to estimate sand, silt, clay ratios.
Step 3 - Chemical Testing: Mix prepared soil with test reagents to determine nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium levels.
Step 4 - Amendment Planning: Calculate organic compost additions to restore depleted mineral reserves within the root zone.

quiz_item.question: How do farming and land-management practices like contour plowing, cover crops, and vegetated riparian buffers along streams protect soil and water resources?
options: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.
C. They compact clay particles into an impermeable crust that prevents groundwater aquifers from recharging.
D. They channel agricultural runoff directly into storm drains to speed up stream erosion downstream.
choices: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.

quiz_item.correct_answer: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.

pamphlet_excerpts: Erosive Detachment: Kinetic energy from falling raindrops breaks open surface soil aggregates upon bare ground.
Sediment Transport: Flowing surface runoff carries suspended silt grains into downstream drainage basins and reservoirs.
Sheet Erosion Pattern: Shallow runoff strips uniform thin layers of fertile topsoil across unprotected hillside slopes.
Gully Incision: Concentrated channel runoff carves deep steep ditches that heavy farm machinery cannot cross.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Site Identification: Locate an active field incision showing visible root exposure and sediment deposition fans.
Step 2 - Erosion Classification: Determine whether detachment occurred through uniform sheet wash, distinct rills, or deep gullies.
Step 3 - Visual Recording: Capture oriented scale photographs and cross section sketches showing active soil loss margins.
Step 4 - Impact Documentation: Record measurable depth metrics and trace sediment deposition paths to nearby drainage ditches.

pamphlet_excerpts: Contour Cultivation: Plowing perpendicular to hillside slope creates micro ridges that retain precipitation on site.
Strip Cropping Benefits: Alternating dense forage grasses with row crops traps dislodged sediment within hillside fields.
Terrace Engineering: Earthen embankments break steep slopes into short steps that dissipate downhill runoff velocity.

pamphlet_excerpts: Topographic Ridges: High ridge elevations define hydrological drainage boundaries separating adjacent precipitation catchment basins.
Nested Drainage: Small tributary sub-watersheds connect continuously to form expansive regional river basin systems.
Basin Interdependence: Upstream chemical discharges and soil tillage degrade water supplies for downstream municipal populations.
Aquifer Confinement: Porous subsurface rock and sand formations store freshwater reserves beneath impermeable geological layers.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Map Orientation: Identify the target stream confluence and study index contour elevations on topographic sheets.
Step 2 - Ridge Delineation: Trace unbroken ridge crests perpendicular to contour lines around the smallest local tributary.
Step 3 - Basin Expansion: Follow high ridgelines outward to delineate the larger collector watershed containing that tributary.
Step 4 - Recharge Analysis: Mark regional aquifer outcrop recharge zones and identify potential contamination threats along rivers.

pamphlet_excerpts: Atmospheric Transport: Solar heat evaporates water into vapor that condenses into clouds and falls as precipitation.
Percolation Movement: Gravity pulls surface water downward through unsaturated soil pore spaces toward the water table.
Vegetation Buffer: Canopy foliage intercepts heavy raindrops while root networks maintain open soil infiltration channels.
Industrial Extraction: Factory cooling systems withdraw large groundwater volumes and risk discharging heated chemical effluent.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Cycle Illustration: Draw the complete hydrologic cycle showing evaporation, condensation, precipitation, transpiration, and infiltration.
Step 2 - Column Assembly: Pack transparent soil columns with dried sand and clay to test water percolation rates.
Step 3 - Capillary Demonstration: Place vertical glass tubes in dyed water to measure upward moisture migration through soil.
Step 4 - Runoff Modeling: Compare water runoff speed and clarity across vegetated turf plots versus bare compacted soil.

pamphlet_excerpts: Contamination Thresholds: Pollutants impair aquatic ecosystems when concentrations exceed natural chemical dilution and assimilation capacities.
Nonpoint Discharges: Stormwater washes motor oil, lawn fertilizers, and road silt into unguarded storm drains.
Primary Settling: Mechanical screens and settling basins remove floating scum and heavy suspended solid matter.
Secondary Digestion: Beneficial aerobic bacteria decompose dissolved organic wastes inside oxygenated municipal aeration tanks.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Watershed Survey: Walk a local shoreline to identify storm drain outfalls and point pollution discharge sources.
Step 2 - Sample Collection: Gather water specimens in sterile containers from both upstream and downstream shoreline locations.
Step 3 - Parameter Testing: Measure dissolved oxygen, turbidity, and chemical nutrient levels to evaluate biochemical oxygen demand.
Step 4 - Treatment Schematics: Draw process diagrams illustrating screening, secondary aerobic digestion, clarifiers, and final chlorination stages.

comparison_data.right_header: Req 6c: Wastewater Treatment Stages and Me
left_points: (6a) Definition of Water Quality Impairment: Water pollution denotes the presence of any physical, chemical, or biological agent that degrades water quality and harms living organisms. It renders water hazardous for drinking, recreation, agricultural irrigation, or wildlife habitat.

(6b) Point and Nonpoint Pollution Sources: Pollution originates from identifiable point sources like industrial pipes and sewage plants, or diffuse nonpoint sources like urban street runoff and fertilized farm fields. Toxic metals poison food chains, excess nutrients cause algae blooms, and silt suffocates fish eggs.
right_points: (6c) Wastewater Treatment Stages and Metrics: Primary treatment physically removes heavy solids through screening and settling, while secondary treatment uses microorganisms to consume dissolved organic waste. Biochemical oxygen demand measures the amount of dissolved oxygen microbes require to break down that organic matter.

(6d) Complete Wastewater Facility Process Diagram: Complete municipal wastewater treatment diagrams depict the sequential flow of sewage through bar screens, grit chambers, primary settling tanks, aeration basins, secondary clarifiers, and disinfection tanks. The schematics show both liquid effluent pathways and solid sludge digestion processes.

rows.left: (6a) Defining Water Pollution: The oxygen is supplied through aeration, that is, by spraying the effluent into the air or by pumping air (p. 78).
rows.right: (6c) Primary Secondary Treatment and BOD: The wastewater repeats all the steps of primary treatment and then one of two processes for further organic waste decomposition (p. 78).

rows.left: (6b) Pollution Sources and Ecological Effects: Often, the effluent resulting from primary treatment requires secondary treatment (p. 78).
rows.right: (6d) Diagramming Complete Wastewater Treatment: Both processes depend on biological action and both require oxygen (p. 78).

rows.left: Oxygen-Dependent Biological Action: Both processes depend on biological action and both require oxygen (p. 78).
rows.right: Step 3 - Route Effluent to Filters: In one process, the effluent goes from the primary settling tank to a trickling filter (p. 78).

fields.Req 6a - Definition of Water Quality Imp: Water pollution denotes the presence of any physical, chemical, or biological agent that degrades water quality and harms living organisms. It renders water hazardous for drinking, recreation, agricultural irrigation, or wildlife habitat.
fields.Req 6b - Point and Nonpoint Pollution So: Pollution originates from identifiable point sources like industrial pipes and sewage plants, or diffuse nonpoint sources like urban street runoff and fertilized farm fields. Toxic metals poison food chains, excess nutrients cause algae blooms, and silt suffocates fish eggs.
fields.Req 6c - Wastewater Treatment Stages and: Primary treatment physically removes heavy solids through screening and settling, while secondary treatment uses microorganisms to consume dissolved organic waste. Biochemical oxygen demand measures the amount of dissolved oxygen microbes require to break down that organic matter.
fields.Req 6d - Complete Wastewater Facility Pr: Complete municipal wastewater treatment diagrams depict the sequential flow of sewage through bar screens, grit chambers, primary settling tanks, aeration basins, secondary clarifiers, and disinfection tanks. The schematics show both liquid effluent pathways and solid sludge digestion processes.

worked_example.sample_output: Water Pollution and Wastewater Treatment: The oxygen is supplied through aeration, that is, by spraying the effluent into the air or by pumping air (p. 78).
worked_example.counselor_tip: For Soil and Water Conservation Requirement 6 (Water Pollution and Wastewater Treatment), verify the Scout's own observations and specific pamphlet details (Official Scouting America Soil and Water Conservation Merit Badge Pamphlet (p. 78, p. 79)).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How does a trickling filter purify wastewater during secondary waste treatment?
quiz_item.question: How does a trickling filter purify wastewater during secondary waste treatment?
options: A. Effluent passes slowly over stones where oxygen-supported biological growths decompose the waste
B. It boils the wastewater under high pressure to evaporate organic solids
C. Giant magnets pull dissolved chemicals out of the primary settling tank
D. Fine sand membranes block all water molecules from passing through
choices: A. Effluent passes slowly over stones where oxygen-supported biological growths decompose the waste
B. It boils the wastewater under high pressure to evaporate organic solids
C. Giant magnets pull dissolved chemicals out of the primary settling tank
D. Fine sand membranes block all water molecules from passing through
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Effluent passes slowly over stones where oxygen-supported biological growths decompose the waste
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In a trickling filter, effluent from the primary settling tank passes slowly over stones or media where aerobic biological growths decompose the remaining organic waste (p. 78).

requirements.description: Do the following: (a) Tell what is meant by water pollution. (b) Describe common sources of water pollution and explain the effects of each. (c) Explain the terms: primary water treatment, secondary waste treatment, and biochemical oxygen demand. (d) Make a drawing showing the principles of complete waste treatment.
requirements.workbook_visual_caption: A hand touches dense surface algae caused by nutrient water pollution.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Water pollution occurs when biological, chemical, or physical contaminants enter aquatic systems and make water unfit for intended natural or municipal uses. Modern treatment facilities use physical screening, microbial digestion, and biochemical monitoring to restore wastewater quality.
socratic_questions: How does decomposing organic sewage deplete dissolved oxygen and cause catastrophic fish kills?
Why are nonpoint agricultural runoff sources harder to regulate and remediate than industrial pipe outfalls?
What critical biological role do aerobic bacteria play during secondary municipal sewage treatment cycles?

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Make a trip to TWO of the following places. Write a report of more than 500 words about the soil and water and energy conservation practices you saw. (1) An agricultural experiment (2) A managed forest or woodlot, range, or pasture (3) A wildlife refuge or a fish or game management area (4) A conservation-managed farm or ranch (5) A managed watershed (6) A waste-treatment plant (7) A public drinking water treatment plant (8) An industry water use installation (9) A desalinization plant (b) Plant 100 trees, bushes, and/or vines for a good purpose. (c) Seed an area of at least one-fifth acre for some worthwhile conservation purposes, using suitable grasses or legumes alone or in a mixture. (d) Study a soil survey report. Describe the things in it. Using tracing paper and a pen, trace over any of the soil maps, and outline an area with three or more different kinds of soil. List each kind of soil by full name and map symbol. (e) Make a list of places in your neighborhood, camps, school ground, or park that have erosion, sedimentation, or pollution problems. Describe how these could be corrected through individual or group action. (f) Carry out any other soil and water conservation project approved by your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Field Inspection: Visiting agricultural research stations reveals cutting-edge crop rotation and irrigation efficiency methods.
Root Stabilization: Planting native shrubs on bare embankments physically binds loose topsoil against rainfall detachment.
Legume Inoculation: Seeding clover or vetch fixes atmospheric nitrogen while blanketing exposed ground with cover.
Survey Mapping: Published county soil surveys identify specific soil limitations and drainage ratings for building.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Project Selection: Select two approved field options such as site visits, planting, or soil surveys.
Step 2 - Site Preparation: Clear competitive weed species and prepare planting beds using hand tools on target ground.
Step 3 - Implementation Execution: Plant seedlings at proper root depth or trace soil boundary maps on drafting paper.
Step 4 - Technical Reporting: Author detailed analytical project reports documenting acreage restored, techniques used, and survival rates.

comparison_data.right_header: Req 7d: County Soil Survey Map Analysis
left_points: (7a) Managed Resource Facility Study Report: Scouts visit two managed facilities such as agricultural research stations, woodlots, or windbreaks to inspect operational conservation systems firsthand. They compose a comprehensive 500-word report analyzing observed soil protection, water management, and energy efficiency measures.

(7b) Erosion Stabilization Seedling Planting Project: Planting 100 trees, shrubs, or vines stabilizes vulnerable soil banks, establishes windbreak barriers, or restores wildlife habitat corridors. Scouts select ecologically suitable native species, dig appropriate root pits, and install protective browse guards.

(7c) Conservation Cover Crop Seeding Execution: Seeding a one-fifth-acre plot with adapted conservation grasses or legumes provides ground cover that halts wind and water erosion. Legumes enrich depleted topsoil with atmospheric nitrogen while deep grass roots restore aggregate stability.
right_points: (7d) County Soil Survey Map Analysis: Scouts study official USDA county soil survey publications to interpret soil capability classes, water tables, and developmental constraints. Using tracing paper, they delineate an area encompassing at least three distinct soil mapping units.

(7e) Community Erosion Remediation Action Plan: Scouts survey local neighborhoods, parks, or school grounds to map active erosion gullies, sediment deposition fans, and polluted runoff points. They formulate practical corrective plans utilizing vegetative buffers, check dams, or mulch stabilization.

(7f) Approved Custom Conservation Stewardship Project: Scouts design and execute an individualized conservation project addressing local soil stability or water quality under counselor guidance. The project involves rigorous planning, active field labor, measurable conservation impact, and documented results.

D. To keep strips of land in permanent vegetation that slow runoff and trap sediment and pollutants

quiz_item.correct_answer: D. To keep strips of land in permanent vegetation that slow runoff and trap sediment and pollutants
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Conservation buffers are small areas or strips kept in permanent vegetation that control erosion and pollution by breaking up and slowing runoff, sediment, and pollutants (p. 49).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do farming and land-management practices like contour plowing, cover crops, and vegetated riparian buffers along streams protect soil and water resources?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do farming and land-management practices like contour plowing, cover crops, and vegetated riparian buffers along streams protect soil and water resources?
options: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.
C. They compact clay particles into an impermeable crust that prevents groundwater aquifers from recharging.
D. They channel agricultural runoff directly into storm drains to speed up stream erosion downstream.
choices: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.
C. They compact clay particles into an impermeable crust that prevents groundwater aquifers from recharging.
D. They channel agricultural runoff directly into storm drains to speed up stream erosion downstream.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Contour farming, cover crops, and streamside buffer strips reduce water velocity, hold topsoil in place against wind and water erosion, and trap sediment and nutrient pollution.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does eroded sediment washed into small streams directly harm game fish populations?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does eroded sediment washed into small streams directly harm game fish populations?
options: A. It raises the water salinity to ocean levels
B. It fills deep dry-season refuge pools, damages spawning beds, and ruins fish eggs
C. It increases dissolved oxygen levels to toxic concentrations
D. It permanently freezes the streambed during summer
choices: A. It raises the water salinity to ocean levels
B. It fills deep dry-season refuge pools, damages spawning beds, and ruins fish eggs
C. It increases dissolved oxygen levels to toxic concentrations
D. It permanently freezes the streambed during summer
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It fills deep dry-season refuge pools, damages spawning beds, and ruins fish eggs
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In small streams, eroded sediment fills deep refuge pools needed during the dry season, damages spawning beds, ruins eggs, and reduces food supplies (p. 39).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why does a severe wildfire on a hillside often cause devastating damage to a downstream city's water supply?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why does a severe wildfire on a hillside often cause devastating damage to a downstream city's water supply?
options: A. Fire turns all hillside bedrock into soluble salt
B. Smoke permanently stops precipitation from falling over the watershed
C. Fire removes protective plant cover, exposing bare soil to beating rains that fill reservoirs with muddy runoff
D. Heat causes underground aquifers to boil dry
choices: A. Fire turns all hillside bedrock into soluble salt
B. Smoke permanently stops precipitation from falling over the watershed
C. Fire removes protective plant cover, exposing bare soil to beating rains that fill reservoirs with muddy runoff
D. Heat causes underground aquifers to boil dry
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Fire removes protective plant cover, exposing bare soil to beating rains that fill reservoirs with muddy runoff
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Fire removes plant cover and exposes bare soil to beating rains, sending heavy muddy runoff down slopes into municipal streams and lakes (p. 45).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does the Soil and Water Conservation pamphlet distinguish between a watershed and a river basin?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does the Soil and Water Conservation pamphlet distinguish between a watershed and a river basin?
options: A. Watersheds only exist in mountains, while river basins only exist on flat plains
B. A watershed holds underground water, while a river basin holds surface water
C. River basins drain into lakes, whereas watersheds drain directly into the ocean
D. All river basins are large watersheds drained by a river and its tributaries, but not all watersheds are large enough to be river basins
choices: A. Watersheds only exist in mountains, while river basins only exist on flat plains
B. A watershed holds underground water, while a river basin holds surface water
C. River basins drain into lakes, whereas watersheds drain directly into the ocean
D. All river basins are large watersheds drained by a river and its tributaries, but not all watersheds are large enough to be river basins
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. All river basins are large watersheds drained by a river and its tributaries, but not all watersheds are large enough to be river basins
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): All river basins are large watersheds drained by a major river and its tributaries, such as the 1-million-square-mile Mississippi River basin, whereas many watersheds are very small (p. 58).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why is evaporation considered one of nature's primary ways of purifying water in the hydrologic cycle?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why is evaporation considered one of nature's primary ways of purifying water in the hydrologic cycle?
options: A. Sunlight boils away bacteria while keeping minerals suspended in the vapor
B. Most dissolved substances, such as the salt in seawater, remain behind when water vapor rises
C. Wind filters out dust particles as water flows into the ocean
D. Clouds chemically neutralize salt using nitrogen gas
choices: A. Sunlight boils away bacteria while keeping minerals suspended in the vapor
B. Most dissolved substances, such as the salt in seawater, remain behind when water vapor rises
C. Wind filters out dust particles as water flows into the ocean
D. Clouds chemically neutralize salt using nitrogen gas
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Most dissolved substances, such as the salt in seawater, remain behind when water vapor rises
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Evaporation purifies water naturally because dissolved substances like the salt in seawater stay behind when solar energy draws water vapor into the atmosphere (p. 30).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does a trickling filter purify wastewater during secondary waste treatment?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a trickling filter purify wastewater during secondary waste treatment?
options: A. Effluent passes slowly over stones where oxygen-supported biological growths decompose the waste
B. It boils the wastewater under high pressure to evaporate organic solids
C. Giant magnets pull dissolved chemicals out of the primary settling tank
D. Fine sand membranes block all water molecules from passing through
choices: A. Effluent passes slowly over stones where oxygen-supported biological growths decompose the waste
B. It boils the wastewater under high pressure to evaporate organic solids
C. Giant magnets pull dissolved chemicals out of the primary settling tank
D. Fine sand membranes block all water molecules from passing through
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Effluent passes slowly over stones where oxygen-supported biological growths decompose the waste
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In a trickling filter, effluent from the primary settling tank passes slowly over stones or media where aerobic biological growths decompose the remaining organic waste (p. 78).

pamphlet_excerpts: Cold War Drivers: Military ballistic missile advancements established foundational boosters for initial crewed orbital flights.
Solar Radiation Data: Heliophysics satellites measure coronal mass ejections to protect commercial power grids.
Spin-off Tech Transfer: Medical imaging sensors directly evolved from charged-coupled devices engineered for orbital observatories.
Global Treaty Frameworks: Outer space accords prohibit national sovereignty claims over planetary bodies and orbits.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Archival Research: Trace military ballistic missile origins to early human spaceflight booster platforms.
Step 2 - Science Mapping: Chart current robotic orbital missions against specific solar system knowledge gaps.
Step 3 - Technology Inventory: Identify three everyday consumer materials derived directly from aerospace engineering programs.
Step 4 - Policy Analysis: Examine international treaty agreements governing cooperative research aboard orbital scientific stations.

left_points: (1a) Space Race Historical Origins: Geopolitical competition between global superpowers accelerated rocket engine development during the mid-twentieth century. Initial orbital launches demonstrated intercontinental ballistic missile capabilities alongside scientific milestones.

(1b) Immediate Planetary Knowledge Goals: Immediate mission objectives prioritize measuring solar radiation, cosmic rays, and planetary atmospheric compositions. These precise physical measurements establish baseline environments for future human voyages.
right_points: (1c) Terrestrial Resource Economic Benefits: Space technology generates consumer spin-offs including scratch-resistant lenses, cordless tools, and advanced water purifiers. Remote sensing satellites monitor freshwater aquifers, agricultural crop health, and deforestation patterns.

(1d) International Outer Space Cooperation: Multinational cooperation enables shared tracking stations, orbital rescue agreements, and distributed development costs. Treaties designate outer space as a global commons for peaceful scientific investigation.

rows.left: Core principles and practical standards for Purposes and Benefits of Space Exploration (p. 69).
rows.right: (1c) Earth Resource and Technology Spinoffs: The United States, Russia, and other countries wanted alarger, longer-lasting facility to do long-term research in space (p. 69).

rows.left: (1b) Immediate Goals in Terms of Specific Knowledge: Purposes of the ISS The million-pound ISS is the largest construction project ever attempted in space (p. 69).
rows.right: (1d) International Cooperation in Space: The space shuttle had supported some research, but flights had been too few and too short (p. 69).

rows.left: Station Data Transmission Support: A bigger space station also would provide better research support services (such as data transmission) than the shuttle could ever provide (p. 69).
rows.right: Step 3 - Identify Core Station Objectives: The International Space Station has several purposes (p. 69).

quiz_item.question: Under the National Association of Rocketry (NAR) Model Rocket Safety Code, how must a model rocket be constructed and launched?
options: A. Build the airframe from lightweight steel tubing and ignite the engine with a hand-held match before stepping back five feet.
B. Pack the parachute directly against the motor nozzle without recovery wadding and launch into low clouds to test altitude.
C. Aim the launch rod horizontally at a 30-degree angle to clear nearby trees and power lines.

D. Use only lightweight non-metallic materials (paper, wood, plastic), install flame-resistant recovery wadding, verify a clear sky and safe standoff distance, and launch electrically using a controller with a removable safety interlock key.
